A way to transform one undirected simple graph into another is by obtaining its subdivision. Intuitively, the subdivision of an undirected graph $\mathrm{G},$ denoted $\text{Sub(G)},$ is the graph formed by taking each edge in $\mathrm{G},$ breaking the edge in half, and joining the two halves together by adding a node into the middle of the edge. For example, here's a graph $\mathrm{G}$ and its subdivision:

Formally speaking, given a graph $\mathrm{G},$ we can form its subdivision $\operatorname{Sub}(G)$ as follows. For each edge $\{u, v\} \in \text{E},$ create a new node $e_{u v}$. Then, replace each edge $\{u, v\}$ with two edges $\left\{u, e_{u v}\right\}$ and $\left\{e_{u v}\right.$, $v\}$. This resulting graph is $\operatorname{Sub(G)}$. (Intuitively, the subdivision of $\mathrm{G}$ is formed by "splitting" each edge into two edges, with a new node inserted in the middle.)

Which of the following is/are true about the subdivision of an undirected simple graph?

options.text: For every undirected simple graph $\mathrm{G},$ the $\operatorname{Sub}(\mathrm{G})$ is always bipartite.
If $\mathrm{G}$ is a planar graph, then $\operatorname{Sub}(\mathrm{G})$ is also planar.
If $\mathrm{G}$ contains an even length cycle then $\operatorname{Sub}(\mathrm{G})$ also contains an even length cycle.
If $\operatorname{Sub}(\mathrm{G})$ contains an even length cycle then $\mathrm{G}$ also contains an even length cycle.

  2. $x \oplus(y \oplus z)=(x \oplus y) \oplus z$ and $x \odot(y \odot z)=(x \odot y) \odot z$.

Also, for each $x$ in $\text{S}$ and for each positive integer $n$, the elements $n x$ and $x^n$ are defined recursively as follows:

  • $1 x=x^1=x$ and
  • if $k x$ and $x^k$ have been defined, then $(k+1) x=k x \oplus x$ and $x^{k+1}=x^k \odot x$.

Which of the following must be true?

  1. $(x \odot y)^n=x^n \odot y^n$ for all $x$ and $y$ in $\text{S}$ and for each positive integer $n$.
  2. $n(x \oplus y)=n x \oplus n y$ for all $x$ and $y$ in $\text{S}$ and for each positive integer $n$.
  3. $x^m \odot x^n=x^{m+n}$ for each $x$ in $\text{S}$ and for all positive integers $m$ and $n$.

Suppose that you have a collection of $n$ Recursively Enumerable ($\mathrm{RE}$) languages $\text{L}_1, \text{L}_2, \ldots, \text{L}_n$ over the same alphabet $\Sigma$ that have the following property: every string in $\Sigma^*$ belongs to exactly one of $\text{L}_1, \text{L}_2, \ldots$, or $\text{L}_n$.

In other words, $\text{L}_1 \cup \text{L}_2 \cup \ldots \cup \text{L}_n=\Sigma^*$, and every string in $\Sigma^*$ belongs to exactly one of the languages $\text{L}_k$.

Which of the following is true for the above $n$ $ \mathrm{RE}$ languages?

options.text: Each of these languages must be undecidable.
Each of these languages must be decidable.
At least one of these languages must be undecidable.
Can't determine decidable/undecidable from the given information.

questions.qtext: Which of the following statements is/are true regarding the pipelining in a processor?

options.text: Pipelining improves performance by decreasing the execution time of an individual instruction.

If the pipelining stages are perfectly balanced (i.e., all stages take the same time), and we have a large number of instructions with no stalls, then the speed-up from pipelining is approximately equal to the number of pipe stages.
The clock cycle (the length of a clock period) in pipelining is determined by the slowest possible stage (the stage with the largest latency).
Assuming no stalls and the same machine instruction set, a $4$-stage pipeline with a cycle time of $125\text{ ps}$ will be faster than a $5$-stage pipeline with a cycle time of $100\text{ ps}.$
